title: Why log score chooses a close density
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Why log score chooses a close density. Rearrange the definition of divergence.
answer: $D(f\Vert\widehat f)=\int f\log f-\int f\log\widehat f$. The first term does not depend on the fitted candidate, leaving the negative expected log score as the comparison.

title: Why training likelihood favours complexity
body: Why training likelihood favours complexity. Identify the missing separation between fitting and assessment.
answer: A larger mixture can reproduce a smaller one, so maximised training likelihood cannot penalise its extra flexibility. Fit on training observations and score held-out observations; an information criterion is another comparison with a complexity penalty.

title: Where the quadratic loses
body: The interpolating quadratic above has penalty integral $8$ and residual sum of squares $0$. For which $\lambda$ is its penalised criterion larger than $2/3$?
answer: The quadratic’s criterion is $8\lambda$. This exceeds $2/3$ when $\lambda>1/12$. At $\lambda=1/12$ the two criteria are equal.

title: What $\lambda=0$ allows
body: At $\lambda=0$, why can a function that passes through every observation achieve a criterion of zero, and why is that function not unique without a further restriction?
answer: The penalty is switched off, and any interpolant has residual sum of squares zero, hence criterion zero. Many smooth functions pass through the same finite set of points. The natural-cubic-spline selection is a property of the penalised problem at $\lambda>0$, not of the unpenalised residual sum of squares.

title: A stable dependence pattern
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

A stable dependence pattern. Calculate the three requested AR(1) summaries.
answer: $\gamma(0)=9/(1-0.4^2)=75/7$, $\gamma(1)=30/7$, and $\rho(2)=0.16$. Stable covariances alone do not supply a calendar season.

title: A forecast depends on its target
body: A forecast depends on its target. Choose the squared-error and absolute-error forecasts.
answer: The conditional mean is $0.8(10)+0.2(30)=14$, which minimises squared error. The conditional median is $10$, which minimises absolute error.

title: Updating five weights
body: One round of AdaBoost: calculate the new error of the same stump.
answer: Only the fifth observation is wrong. Its initial weight is $0.2$, giving $\alpha=\tfrac12\log4$. Multipliers are $1/2$ on correct points and $2$ on the error; after division by $0.8$, the weights are $(1/8,1/8,1/8,1/8,1/2)$. The same stump therefore has new error $1/2$.

title: Identical classifiers
body: A tempting wrong turn: explain why replicating one deterministic rule does not improve its prediction.
answer: All member predictions coincide, so their average is the same prediction. Their diversity is zero and their pairwise correlation is one whenever the variance is positive. Random forests vary samples and candidate predictors; AdaBoost changes weights across rounds. Each approach changes the fitted members rather than merely repeating one rule.

title: Rewrite the hidden update
body: Delta form asks for the factored derivative.
answer: Substitute $2(y-o)o(1-o)=-\delta^{(o)}$ into the hidden-weight update. The remaining sum multiplied by $h(1-h)$ is $\delta^{(h)}$, giving $\Delta w_{ab}=-\varepsilon\sum_i\delta_{ib}^{(h)}x_{ia}$.

title: Check all factors in a scalar derivative
body: A gradient by hand gives a numerical comparison.
answer: For $x=2,y=0,w_0=0,w_1=1$, $o=g(2)=0.880797$ and $\partial E/\partial w_1=4o^2(1-o)=0.369912$. A central difference with step $0.001$ agrees to the stated rounding. Omitting $e^{-z}$ in the exponential form gives approximately $2.7333$ instead.

title: On the four-point dendrogram, how many clusters does a cut at height $0.5$ return, and how many does a cut at height $7$ return?
body: On the four-point dendrogram, how many clusters does a cut at height $0.5$ return, and how many does a cut at height $7$ return?
answer: Height $0.5$ is below every merge, so there are four clusters, the four points. Height $7$ is above the last merge at $6$, so there is one cluster.

title: Why is the single-linkage distance from $\{0,1\}$ to $4$ equal to $3$ rather than $4$?
body: Why is the single-linkage distance from $\{0,1\}$ to $4$ equal to $3$ rather than $4$?
answer: Single linkage takes the closest pair across the two groups. That pair is $1$ and $4$, at distance $3$. The distance $4$ is the complete-linkage height, using $0$ and $4$.

title: Facial tumours in Tasmanian devils
body: Thirty devils are split into two groups of 15. One group is given a medicine. What must the description still say before the split can be judged as a randomised experiment, and what is the response?
answer: The split is an experiment once the investigators assign the medicine. Judging the comparison needs the allocation rule, whether measurement was blind, whether the untreated devils had the same handling, and whether the groups were comparable at the start. The response is the change in tumour size over 12 weeks, or the later size adjusted for the starting size. It is quantitative. The medicine-or-not factor is categorical with two levels.

title: A dose comparison for middle-of-the-night insomnia
body: Twenty-four patients are randomly allocated to placebo, a low dose, or a high dose. What kind of study is this, and what type of variable is the dose?
answer: It is a randomised designed experiment with a placebo control. Dose takes three named levels, so it is categorical. The levels have an order, so the factor is ordinal. Total sleep time, the response, is a duration and is quantitative. The random allocation is what makes a later difference in sleep a comparison of the assigned doses.

title: Birth–death stationary weights
body: A birth–death chain on $\{0,1,2\}$ has $p_0=1$, $q_1=1/3$, $p_1=2/3$ and $q_2=1$. Using $\pi_i p_i=\pi_{i+1} q_{i+1}$, find $\pi$.
answer: $\pi_0\cdot 1=\pi_1\cdot(1/3)$, so $\pi_1=3\pi_0$. Then $\pi_1\cdot(2/3)=\pi_2\cdot 1$, so $\pi_2=(2/3)\cdot 3\pi_0=2\pi_0$. The sum is $\pi_0(1+3+2)=6\pi_0=1$, hence $\pi=(1/6,\ 1/2,\ 1/3)$. Each edge flow matches by construction.

title: A path graph
body: Why does the deterministic three-cycle fail detailed balance even though $(1/3,1/3,1/3)$ is stationary?
answer: The forward edge has probability 1 and the reverse edge has probability 0, so the products $(1/3)\cdot 1$ and $(1/3)\cdot 0$ differ. Stationarity only asks that the total mass into each state equal $1/3$. It does not ask the mass to return along the same edge.

title: The saturated comparison
body:
Keep unscaled deviance distinct from its dispersion-scaled likelihood ratio.

Saturated model and deviance: which squared residual sum corresponds to $D$, and which to $D/\phi$?
answer: The unit-deviance residuals satisfy $\sum_i r_{D,i}^2=D$. Their dispersion-scaled versions $r_{D,i}/\sqrt\phi$ satisfy a squared sum of $D/\phi$, the scaled likelihood-ratio discrepancy at the common dispersion.

title: Comparing fitted models
body: Reading the deviance: use the stated Wald approximation to predict the reduced-model deviance.
answer: The approximate increase is $1.016^2=1.032256$, giving $354.97+1.032256\approx356.0023$ on $297$ residual degrees of freedom. The actual observed likelihood-ratio difference requires refitting the reduced model. The approximation is below the supplied one-degree-of-freedom critical value $3.84$.

title: Both rows of a two-state matrix equal $(1/2,1/2)$.
body: Both rows of a two-state matrix equal $(1/2,1/2)$. What is the two-step probability of moving from state $1$ to state $2$?
answer: Every one-step probability into state $2$ is $1/2$, so the two-step probability is $(1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/2)=1/2$. The square of this matrix equals the matrix itself.

title: Successive states of a Markov chain are not automatically independent.
body: Successive states of a Markov chain are not automatically independent. For the worked matrix above, why is state $2$ more likely after state $2$ than after state $1$?
answer: The second row puts probability $0.5$ on staying in state $2$, while the first row puts only $0.2$ there. Different rows mean the next state still carries information about the current state.

title: Signed distances
body:
Use the normal direction and the boundary equation to check these calculations.

Distance to a hyperplane: calculate the signed distances of $(2,1)$ and $(0,0)$ when $w=(3,4)^\top$, $b=-5$.
answer: The scores are $5$ and $-5$, and the normal has length $5$. The signed distances are $1$ and $-1$. The score planes at $\pm1$ are $0.4$ apart.

title: The geometry of two support points
body: A two-point machine: for opposite labels at $(3,3)$ and $(1,1)$, check the margin of $w=(1/2,1/2)$ and $b=-2$.
answer: The two scores are $1$ and $-1$, and $\|w\|=1/\sqrt2$. The total margin is $2\sqrt2$, equal to the distance between the two points. The dual multiplier for either point is $1/4$.

title: An affine exponential transformation
body: An affine exponential transformation
answer: For $X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1/2)$ and $Y=1+2X$, substitute $x=(y-1)/2$ and multiply by $1/2$. The result is $e^{-(y-1)/4}/4$ on $[1,\infty)$.

title: Two independent exponentials
body: Two independent exponentials
answer: The density $2e^{-x-2y}$ on the positive quadrant factors into exponential densities with rates one and two. Independence gives $E(XY)=1/2$. Also $\operatorname{Cov}(X+Y,X-Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)-\operatorname{Var}(Y)=1-1/4=3/4$.

title: Column sums
body:
Check both the matrix sums and the behaviour from the stated initial law.

A doubly stochastic matrix: prove uniform invariance directly.
answer: For each destination $j$, $(uP)_j=m^{-1}\sum_iP_{ij}=m^{-1}$. Thus every coordinate of $uP$ agrees with $u$.

title: A three-cycle
body: A deterministic three-cycle: what is the probability of returning to the initial state after $n$ steps?
answer: It equals one when $n$ is divisible by three and zero otherwise. Its failure to converge is compatible with the uniform distribution being stationary.

title: Why a quadratic form is nonnegative
body:
The matrix properties behind quadratic optimisation appear in these two calculations.

Why a covariance is positive semi-definite: connect a covariance quadratic form with the Gram-matrix requirement in the classifier dual.
answer: The covariance quadratic form is a variance and is nonnegative. A Gram quadratic form similarly equals a squared norm: $a^TGa=\|\sum_i a_ix_i\|^2\geq0$. Multiplying coordinates by labels preserves this property, giving the concavity of the negative quadratic term in the dual.

title: Making a quadratic strictly convex
body: Ridge makes the matrix invertible: find the two eigenvalues before adding the ridge penalty and the fitted coefficient vector afterwards.
answer: The matrix $X^TX$ has eigenvalues four and zero. Adding $I$ gives eigenvalues five and one, making the quadratic strictly convex. With the supplied response, the ridge estimate is $(4/5,4/5)^T$.

title: Read the reference cell
body: Level 1 of each factor is the reference, and the estimates are $\hat\mu=10$, $\hat\alpha_2=4$, $\hat\beta_2=-2$, and $\hat\gamma_{22}=3$. Write the four cell means. What is the change in moving factor A from level 1 to level 2 when factor B is at level 2?
answer: The means are $10$ at $(1,1)$, $10-2=8$ at $(1,2)$, $10+4=14$ at $(2,1)$, and $10+4-2+3=15$ at $(2,2)$. The move in A at level 2 of B changes the mean by $4+3=7$, from $8$ to $15$. The main effect $4$ is that change only at the reference level of B.

title: An interaction sum of squares
body: Cell means in a $2\times 2$ table, one observation each, are $3,5$ in the first row and $4,10$ in the second. Compute the interaction sum of squares.
answer: The row means are $4$ and $7$, the column means are $3.5$ and $7.5$, and the grand mean is $5.5$. The interaction residuals are $1,-1,-1,1$, and the sum of squares is $4$. With one observation per cell there is no residual degree of freedom left for an error mean square.

title: A monotone validation curve
body: Validation errors are $0.40$, $0.33$, $0.29$, $0.27$, $0.26$. Where does the rule stop?
answer: The minimum on this list is the last value, $0.26$, so the rule keeps the fifth epoch. A validation curve that has not turned up does not, by itself, say that a later epoch would be worse. It only says that, among the epochs already run, the last one is best.

title: Training versus validation
body: At epoch $4$ the training error is $0.14$ and the validation error is $0.29$. At epoch $3$ the training error is $0.21$ and the validation error is $0.27$. Which epoch does early stopping keep?
answer: Epoch $3$, because $0.27<0.29$. The lower training error at epoch $4$ is the quantity the rule is refusing to chase.

title: One change in a trace
body: A stored series has $n=400$ and geometric autocorrelation $\rho=0.5$. Using the long-run formula, what is $n_{\mathrm{eff}}$?
answer: $(1-0.5)/(1+0.5)=1/3$, so $n_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx400/3=133.33$. The variance of the mean is about three times the independent-draw variance. The exact finite-sample inflation is a little different, because the factors $(1-k/n)$ have been replaced by 1.

title: A posterior mean
body: Why can two posterior summaries from the same chain have different effective sample sizes?
answer: Each summary is a function $g(X_t)$. The autocorrelations of $g(X_t)$ need not equal the autocorrelations of $X_t$. The variance inflation is computed from the series actually averaged. A precise mean does not imply a precise tail probability.

title: A numerical E-step
body: A numerical E-step
answer: At $x=1$, equal-weight unit-variance components centred at zero and two have equal densities. Each responsibility is therefore $1/2$.

title: A numerical M-step
body: A numerical M-step
answer: For observations zero and two with first-component responsibilities $0.75$ and $0.25$, each component has effective count one. The weights are $1/2$ and the weighted means are $0.5$ and $1.5$.

title: Hyperparameter uncertainty
body: Hyperparameter uncertainty
answer: An equal mixture of $N(5,1)$ and $N(9,1)$ has mean seven. Total variance is the within-component variance one plus the variance four of the two component means, giving five.

title: A beta-binomial hierarchy
body: A beta-binomial hierarchy
answer: At fixed hyperparameters $(2,8)$, the studies with counts $(4,10)$ and $(40,100)$ have posteriors Beta$(6,14)$ and Beta$(42,68)$, with means $0.3$ and $21/55$. The prior receives weights $1/2$ and $1/11$. With unknown positive hyperparameters and independent Exp$(1)$ priors, their posterior kernel is $e^{-\alpha-\beta}B(\alpha,\beta)^{-J}\prod_jB(\alpha+y_j,\beta+n_j-y_j)$.

title: A Gaussian kernel estimate
body: A Gaussian kernel estimate
answer: For observations $(-1,0,2)$ and bandwidth one, the Gaussian-kernel estimate at zero is $[\phi(1)+\phi(0)+\phi(2)]/3\approx0.231635$.

title: Why a multivariate kernel estimate integrates to one
body: Why a multivariate kernel estimate integrates to one
answer: For each summand use $u=H^{-1/2}(x-X_i)$. Its Jacobian is $|H|^{1/2}$, cancelling the scaling $|H|^{-1/2}$. Each kernel integrates to one and averaging preserves that integral.

title: Batch versus online
body: A training set has $5000$ cases. How many online updates equal one epoch, and how many batch updates equal one epoch?
answer: Online learning updates after every case, so one epoch is $5000$ updates. Batch learning updates once from the full sum, so one epoch is $1$ update.

title: A remainder
body: With $n=20$ and $m=4$, a run stops after $7$ updates. How many full epochs have finished, and how many batches of the next epoch have been used?
answer: Five updates finish the first epoch. The next two updates are two of the five batches of the second epoch. The run has completed $1$ epoch and $2/5$ of the next, which is $7/5=1.4$ epochs.

title: A correlation four visits cannot have
body: A correlation four visits cannot have
answer: Four visits require $\rho\ge-1/3$. At $-0.5$ the mean-direction eigenvalue is negative, so the proposed matrix is impossible.

title: Working correlation and mean validity
body: Working correlation and mean validity
answer: With many independent clusters, regularity and suitable missingness, the analyst with the correct marginal mean has the usual GEE consistency argument even with a wrong working correlation. A sandwich estimates uncertainty about that estimating equation. It cannot repair an omitted mean covariate.

title: Fair success and duration
body: A fair walk on eight steps: calculate both quantities from its start at five.
answer: The upper-boundary probability is $5/8$. The expected duration until either boundary is $5(8-5)=15$ steps. One is a probability, the other a mean number of transitions.

title: Checking the quadratic
body: Checking the duration formula: verify the recurrence directly.
answer: Both endpoints of $e_x=x(d-x)$ are zero. Expanding the two neighbouring values gives $(e_{x+1}+e_{x-1})/2=x(d-x)-1$. Adding one therefore returns $e_x$, exactly the fair-walk first-step equation.

title: Recover the class probability
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Recover the class probability. Evaluate the requested half-logit.
answer: $f^*=\tfrac12\log4=\log2$ and $1/(1+e^{-2f^*})=0.8$. At probability $0.5$, $f^*=0$.

title: One AdaBoost round
body: One AdaBoost round. Compute the updated mass on the error.
answer: The weighted error is $0.2$, the coefficient is $\log2$, and the normaliser is $0.8$. The mistaken observation has new weight $0.5$, making this same stump wrong on half the new weight.

title: Scale an exponential maximum
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Scale an exponential maximum. Give the requested rate-two sequences.
answer: Use $b_n=(\log n)/2$ and $a_n=1/2$. Then $2b_n=\log n$ and $2a_n=1$, leaving the exceedance probability $e^{-x}/n$.

title: Build the exact distribution
body: Build the exact distribution. Use the event that every observation is below the threshold.
answer: Independence gives $\Pr(M\le u)=\prod_{i=1}^n F_i(u)$. With a common distribution this is $F(u)^n$.

title: Offspring probabilities $p_0=1/8$, $p_1=1/8$, $p_2=3/4$.
body: Offspring probabilities $p_0=1/8$, $p_1=1/8$, $p_2=3/4$. Is the mean above $1$?
answer: The mean is $1/8+2\cdot 3/4=1/8+3/2=13/8>1$. Extinction is not certain. The probability itself is the smaller root of $f(s)=s$, not the mean.

title: If $p_0=0$ and $p_2=1$, what is the extinction probability, and what is the mean?
body: If $p_0=0$ and $p_2=1$, what is the extinction probability, and what is the mean?
answer: Every individual has two children, so the mean is $2$ and generation $n$ has size $2^n$. The process never hits $0$, and the extinction probability is $0$. The root $s=0$ of $f(s)=s^2$ is that probability.

title: A larger exponential sample
body: Compute $(1-1/50)^{50}$ and say whether it is closer to $e^{-1}=0.36788$ than $(1-1/20)^{20}=0.35849$ is.
answer: $(1-1/50)^{50}=0.36417$. The gap to $0.36788$ is $0.00371$, smaller than the gap $0.00939$ at $n=20$. The limit statement is visible in the arithmetic.

title: Which type has a finite upper end?
body: A measurement cannot exceed $1$, and one studies $n(1-M_n)$. Which of the three types is that limit, and why is it not Gumbel?
answer: It is the Weibull extreme-value type. The maximum is pressed against a finite endpoint, so the limiting variable lives on one side of $0$. A Gumbel limit is spread over the whole real line and comes from an unbounded light tail, not from a hard ceiling.

title: Checking equal variances
body: Checking equal variances
answer: For two independent normal samples of size fifty with standard deviations $14.1$ and $14.3$, the observed ratio is about $0.97222$. Using the supplied critical value $1.762$ gives the interval $(0.55177,1.71306)$ approximately. It contains one, indicating compatibility with equality at that confidence level, rather than proving it.

title: Expectation of sample variance
body: Expectation of sample variance
answer: Expand about the population mean to obtain $\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2=\sum(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X-\mu)^2$. Expectations give $n\sigma^2-\sigma^2=(n-1)\sigma^2$, hence the sample variance with divisor $n-1$ is unbiased.

title: Two factors of one covariance
body: Two factors of one covariance
answer: For $\Sigma=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}4&2\\2&3\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, the Cholesky factor is $L=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&0\\1&\sqrt2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. A spectral factor also satisfies $BB^T=\Sigma$. Both transform a standard normal vector to covariance $\Sigma$, although they need not give the same transformed vector for a fixed draw.

title: The effect of correlation
body: The effect of correlation
answer: For $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&r\\r&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $r>0$, the eigenvalues are $1+r$ and $1-r$, along the sum and difference directions. The first principal component explains fraction $(1+r)/2$, tending to $1/2$ as $r\to0$ and to one as $r\to1$.

title: Sorted $p$-values $0.01$ and $0.04$, with $M=2$ and level $0.05$.
body: Sorted $p$-values $0.01$ and $0.04$, with $M=2$ and level $0.05$. How many hypotheses are rejected?
answer: The thresholds are $0.025$ and $0.05$. Then $0.01<0.025$ and $0.04<0.05$, so both are rejected.

title: In that two-test rejection, could the realised false-discovery proportion still be $1$?
body: In that two-test rejection, could the realised false-discovery proportion still be $1$?
answer: Yes. If both nulls are true, then $V=R=2$ and the proportion is $1$. Control of the expected proportion does not cap the proportion on a single list.

title: A fair walk between 0 and 8
body: A fair walk is absorbed at $0$ and at $8$, and starts at $5$. Find the probability of reaching $8$ before $0$, and the expected absorption time.

title: A biased walk on four steps
body: Take $p=2/3$, barriers at $0$ and $4$, and a start at $1$. Compute the probability of hitting $4$ before $0$, and compare it with the fair-walk value.
answer: $q/p=1/2$, so $h_1=(1-1/2)/(1-(1/2)^4)=(1/2)/(15/16)=8/15$. The fair value is $1/4$. Because $8/15>1/4$, the upward drift lifts the hitting probability above the fair line.

title: A smaller conditional experiment
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

A smaller conditional experiment. List the top-left counts and compute the upper tail.
answer: The possible counts are $0,1,2,3$. At three, the mass is $\binom43\binom30/\binom73=4/35$. No larger count is possible, so the one-sided tail is also $4/35$.

title: Identify the sampling design
body: Identify the sampling design. Distinguish the fixed and random margins.
answer: The two-drug trial fixes treatment totals and tests homogeneity of improvement probabilities. The clinic survey fixes only its total and tests independence of classifications. The factories fix factory totals and test homogeneity of defective probabilities.

title: Comparing two directions
body: Fisher's direction: compare the optimal and raw-contrast criteria.
answer: With $d=(-3,-2)^\top$ and the displayed covariance, $S^{-1}d=(-3/2,-3/2)^\top$. The maximum is $d^\top S^{-1}d/2=15/4=3.75$. Using $a=d$ gives $a^\top Sa=68/3$ and $J(d)=507/136\approx3.727941$, which is smaller.

title: Covariance parameters and rank
body: Parameter counts: count the parameters for three classes and ten predictors.
answer: There are $30$ mean parameters and two free prior probabilities. A symmetric ten-dimensional covariance has $55$ parameters. LDA therefore has $30+55+2=87$ and QDA has $30+3(55)+2=197$. Each QDA class needs at least $11$ observations whose centred predictor vectors span ten dimensions; the count alone does not guarantee nonsingularity.

title: Summaries of ten cartons
body: For the ten milk-carton volumes $0.998$, $1.019$, $1.035$, $1.037$, $1.041$, $1.051$, $1.068$, $1.077$, $1.084$, and $1.102$, the lower quartile is defined as the median of the five values below the sample median, and the upper quartile as the median of the five above it. Report the median and the two quartiles.
answer: The ordered sample has ten values, so the median is $(1.041+1.051)/2=1.046$. The lower quartile is $1.035$ and the upper quartile is $1.077$. This hinge rule is not the $(n+1)/4$ formula, and the two recipes need not agree.

title: Skewness beside the boxplot
body: Serum creatinine in the same cohort has moment skewness about $4.4$ on the original scale and $1.6$ after logarithms. Does the smaller skewness prove that the log measurements are normal?
answer: No. The drop from about $4.4$ to $1.6$ still leaves positive moment skewness, and a skewness of zero would not imply normality either. A histogram or a normal quantile plot is needed to look at the shape.

title: Costs of cross-validation
body: Costs of cross-validation
answer: For $n=1000$, leave-one-out needs $1000$ fold fits and ten-fold needs ten. Adding one final all-data fit gives $1001$ and $11$, respectively. With ten outer folds, nine inner folds and five candidates, inner selection plus one outer refit costs $10(9\cdot5+1)=460$. The stated final ten-fold selection and refit add $10\cdot5+1=51$, giving $511$.

title: Separate tuning from evaluation
body: Separate tuning from evaluation
answer: Choosing the highest validation accuracy among twenty candidates selects favourable sampling noise as well as good performance. Fit preprocessing inside training, select on validation data, freeze the choices, refit if desired, and assess on an independent test set. If cross-validation tunes the models, an external test set or an outer loop must assess that tuning procedure.

title: A critical offspring law
body: Offspring probabilities are $2/5$, $1/5$ and $2/5$ on $0$, $1$ and $2$. What are the mean and the extinction probability?
answer: The mean is $1/5+4/5=1$. The law is non-degenerate and $p_0>0$, so the extinction probability is 1. The equation $f(s)=s$ has a double root at 1 and no root in $[0,1)$.

title: The variance recurrence
body: For the two-or-none law, $m=3/2$ and $\sigma^2=3/4$. Check $\Var(Z_1)$ and $\Var(Z_2)$ from the displayed formula.
answer: At $n=1$ the formula returns $\sigma^2=3/4=0.75$. At $n=2$ it returns $(3/4)\cdot(3/2)\cdot((9/4)-1)/(1/2)=45/16=2.8125$. The recurrence $\Var(Z_2)=m^2\Var(Z_1)+\sigma^2 m$ gives $(9/4)(3/4)+(3/4)(3/2)=27/16+9/8=45/16$, the same value.

title: Differentiating a link
body: The logistic derivative: practise the link differentiation used in GLM scores.
answer: For $\sigma(\eta)=(1+e^{-\eta})^{-1}$, differentiation gives $\sigma'(\eta)=e^{-\eta}/(1+e^{-\eta})^2=\sigma(\eta)(1-\sigma(\eta))$. Also $\sigma(-\eta)=1-\sigma(\eta)$. Thus a Bernoulli logit model has Hessian $-X^\top\operatorname{diag}(p_i(1-p_i))X$; the gamma log-link Hessian uses different weights.

title: Interpreting a variance divisor
body: The biased variance estimator: distinguish an estimator's scale from its bias.
answer: Since $E(s^2)=\sigma^2$, $E(((n-1)/n)s^2)=(n-1)\sigma^2/n$. Its bias is $-\sigma^2/n$. Changing a residual divisor affects estimation of dispersion, even when the fitted mean coefficients stay the same.

title: Precision to graph
body: For $K=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&3&-1\\0&-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, identify the graph and the partial correlation on each edge.
answer: The graph is $1-2-3$ and both edge partial correlations equal $1/\sqrt6$. Its inverse is $\frac18\left(\begin{smallmatrix}5&2&1\\2&4&2\\1&2&5\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, whose $(1,3)$ entry is nonzero.

title: A three-variable chain
body: What is the covariance between the endpoints when the two transition coefficients are $0.8$ and each coordinate has variance one?
answer: It is $0.8^2=0.64$. Conditioning on the middle coordinate removes that endpoint association; the precision entry $k_{13}$ is zero.

title: Normal equations
body: In the four-point example, why does a slope of 0.6 with standard error 0.1414 fail to reject at the 5% level?
answer: The ratio is $0.6/0.1414=4.243$. The $0.975$ quantile of $t_2$ is 4.3027. Because $4.243<4.3027$, the level-0.05 two-sided test does not reject a zero slope. The comparison uses two residual degrees of freedom. A normal critical value near 1.96 would have rejected, and that is not the Gaussian model's reference law here.

title: Normal–inverse-$\chi^2$ regression
body: The sampling model says $\hat\beta$ is normal. What extra ingredient makes a posterior for $\beta$ normal–inverse-chi-squared rather than a sampling distribution?
answer: A prior distribution on $(\beta,\sigma^2)$. The Gaussian linear model by itself is the distribution of $Y$ given those parameters. Putting a normal–inverse-chi-squared prior on them, and conditioning on $Y$, produces a posterior in the same family. The least-squares fit is the posterior mode or mean only for particular priors. It is not automatically a posterior summary.

title: Check a proposed covariance
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Check a proposed covariance. Apply the nonnegative-variance condition.
answer: For any coefficient vector $a$, $a^\top\Sigma a$ is a variance. The displayed candidate correlation matrix has determinant $-2.888$, so it cannot be a covariance matrix.

title: Uncorrelated coordinates need a joint assumption
body: Uncorrelated coordinates need a joint assumption. Explain the dependence in the example.
answer: For a centred standard normal $X$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,X^2)=\mathbb E(X^3)=0$, but the second coordinate is determined by the first. This vector is not jointly Gaussian.

title: Two normal means
body: Two groups each have eight observations, known variance four, and means twelve and fifteen. Find the between-group sum of squares and the likelihood-ratio statistic.
answer: The pooled mean is $13.5$. Thus $SS_B=8(12-13.5)^2+8(15-13.5)^2=36$, and $D=36/4=9$. It exceeds the stated $3.84$ cutoff.

title: How many restrictions?
body: For an intercept, nitrogen, phosphorus and their product, how many independent restrictions remove all three non-intercept terms?
answer: Three. Set each of those three coefficients to zero; the intercept remains free under the null.

title: Patient-specific trends
body: Random slopes and changed conclusions: describe the extra random coefficient and compare the two interaction uncertainties.
answer: Add $b_{1i}t$ to the patient intercept $b_{0i}$ and give $(b_{0i},b_{1i})$ a joint centred normal law with a positive semidefinite covariance matrix. The interaction statistics change from $-0.080/0.030\approx-2.667$ to $-0.070/0.055\approx-1.273$. The second standard error is larger, so its estimated difference is less precisely determined. Its approximate interval is $-0.070\pm1.96(0.055)=(-0.1778,0.0378)$, which includes nonzero differences as well as zero.

title: Dependence from a patient intercept
body: Toenail infection GLMM: explain why random allocation does not remove repeated-measure dependence.
answer: Repeated visits share the same patient's latent intercept. The conditional logit includes treatment, week, their interaction and that intercept. Given the intercept the visits are modelled as independent; marginally their probabilities covary through it. Random treatment assignment addresses the treatment comparison but does not make repeated measurements from a person independent.

title: Row sums
body: What do the two rows of the rate-$2$ and rate-$4$ generator sum to?
answer: Each row sums to $0$: $-2+2=0$ and $4-4=0$.

title: Time versus visits
body: With those rates, what fraction of visits does the jump chain spend idle, and what fraction of time does the continuous-time chain spend idle?
answer: The jump chain alternates, so half of the visits are idle. The time average is $2/3$, because idle spells last twice as long as busy spells.

title: One hour
body: Starting idle, about how large is the probability of being busy after one hour, and what is the stationary value it is approaching?
answer: The probability is $(1-e^{-6})/3\approx 0.3325$. The stationary probability of busy is $1/3\approx 0.3333$.

title: Prove the density version
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Prove the density version. Apply the logarithm inequality under the true distribution.
answer: Integrating $-\log(\widehat f/f)\ge1-\widehat f/f$ against $f$ gives a nonnegative divergence. Equality requires agreement almost everywhere; the expected log-score identity follows by expanding the logarithm.

title: Distinguish fitted and future likelihood
body: Distinguish fitted and future likelihood. Identify why a more flexible training fit does not settle prediction.
answer: Nested models can reproduce the smaller fit, making maximum training likelihood nondecreasing with flexibility. Prediction requires an assessment that accounts for fitting, such as held-out likelihood or an appropriate complexity penalty.

title: A pure node
body: All $10$ cases in a node belong to one class. What is the Gini index?
answer: One proportion is $1$ and the others are $0$, so $1-\sum\hat p_g^2=0$. Two draws from the node always match.

title: The even two-class node
body: For two classes with $p=1/2$, what is $2p(1-p)$?
answer: $2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac12$. This is the largest two-class value: the quadratic $2p(1-p)$ opens downwards and its vertex is at $p=1/2$.

title: A deterministic cycle
body: For the cycle $1\to 2\to 3\to 1$ and $\pi=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$, compute one global-balance residual and one detailed-balance residual.
answer: At state 1 the incoming mass is $\pi_3 p_{31}=1/3$ and $\pi_1=1/3$, so the global residual is 0. On the edge from 1 to 2 the products are $1/3$ and 0, so the detailed residual is $1/3$.

title: Doubly stochastic matrices
body: Why does every doubly stochastic matrix have the uniform distribution as a stationary distribution, and why is that not detailed balance?
answer: If every column sums to 1 and $\pi_i=1/m$ for $m$ states, then $(\pi P)_j=(1/m)\sum_i p_{ij}=1/m$. That is global balance. Detailed balance also needs $p_{ij}=p_{ji}$ when $\pi$ is uniform. A permutation cycle has $p_{ij}\neq p_{ji}$ and is still doubly stochastic.

title: One round of AdaBoost
body: One round of AdaBoost
answer: One error among five equally weighted observations gives $\epsilon=0.2$ and $a=\log2$. Correct observations receive unnormalised weight $0.1$ each and the error receives $0.4$, with normaliser $0.8$. The resulting weights are $0.125$ for each correct case and $0.5$ for the incorrect case; the same stump then has weighted error $0.5$.

title: How ensemble members differ
body: How ensemble members differ
answer: Bagging changes training samples through bootstrap resampling. Random forests also randomise the candidate variables at tree splits. AdaBoost changes observation weights sequentially and combines weighted learners, directing later fits toward cases that the current ensemble handles poorly.

title: A diagonal feature map
body: Two inputs map to $\phi(x_1)=(2,0)$ and $\phi(x_2)=(0,3)$. Write the Gram matrix and its eigenvalues.
answer: The products are $4$, $0$ and $9$, so $K_S=\operatorname{diag}(4,9)$. The eigenvalues are $4$ and $9$. The off-diagonal zeros record orthogonal features.

title: A coefficient that cancels
body: Using the three-point matrix in the worked example, take $c=(1,1,-1)^\top$. Compute $c^\top K_S c$, and say what that number means for the mapped points.
answer:
$$
c^\top K_S c=\bigl\|(1,0)+(0,1)-(1,1)\bigr\|^2=\|(0,0)\|^2=0.
$$


The three feature vectors with these coefficients sum to the zero vector, so the quadratic form contributes nothing even though $c$ itself is not zero.

title: Thresholding correlations
body:
Distinguish a marginal association from a conditional association.

A tempting wrong turn: why does thresholding a correlation matrix fail to estimate Gaussian conditional independences directly?
answer: Marginal correlations belong to the covariance matrix, whereas Gaussian conditional independences correspond to zeros of the precision matrix. A sparse precision model estimates the latter pattern while respecting positive definiteness.

title: Reading the precision matrix
body: Conditional association and sparsity: interpret the zeros and calculate its two partial correlations.
answer: The graph has edges $1$–$2$ and $2$–$3$. Coordinates $1$ and $3$ are conditionally independent given coordinate $2$. With diagonal entries one, the two partial correlations are $0.2$ and $-0.3$. Marginal association between coordinates $1$ and $3$ can still arise through coordinate $2$.

title: Sampling a two-dimensional table
body: Sampling from a two-dimensional grid: obtain 100 independent cell draws.
answer: Normalise the nonnegative cell weights, flatten the table and compute cumulative probabilities. For each of 100 fresh independent uniforms, select the first cumulative probability at least as large as the uniform and map its index back to the two grid coordinates. Optional within-cell jitter changes the representation inside cells, while preserving their probabilities.

title: A discrete credible set
body: A discrete highest-probability set: find a smallest set with at least 80% posterior probability.
answer: For probabilities $(0.5,0.3,0.2)$ on $(1,2,3)$, the set $\{1,2\}$ has probability $0.8$. No singleton reaches the target. Discrete probability jumps can make other target levels unattainable exactly, and tied probabilities require a selection convention.

title: Interpreting multipliers
body: Interpreting multipliers
answer: For soft-margin $C=2$, a zero multiplier implies zero slack and margin at least one. A multiplier $1.3$ lies strictly between zero and $C$, hence has margin one and zero slack and can determine the intercept. A multiplier equal to $C$ has margin at most one and slack $1-yf$, possibly zero; its multiplier alone does not determine the slack.

title: Kernel as an inner product
body: Kernel as an inner product
answer: With $\phi(x)=(1,\sqrt2x,x^2)$, the inner product is $1+2xx'+x^2x'^2=(1+xx')^2$. Middle observations with $|x|\le0.9$ have squared coordinate at most $0.81$; tails with $|x|\ge1.5$ have squared coordinate at least $2.25$. A threshold $1.53$ in that coordinate separates them with equal coordinate gaps $0.72$.

title: A keen reverse jump
body: Using $p(1)=0.2$, $p(3)=0.5$, $J(1\mid 3)=0.4$ and $J(3\mid 1)=0.1$, find $r$ for a move from $1$ to $3$.
answer:
$$
r=\frac{0.5\times 0.4}{0.2\times 0.1}=10.
$$
The acceptance probability is $1$. The proposal rarely offers the move, and the target density is higher at the destination, so the correction makes the ratio larger than $1$.

title: Where the correction is idle
body: A proposal adds an increment drawn from $N(0,1)$, independent of the sign. What is the Hastings correction?
answer: The increment density is symmetric, so $J(\omega+d\mid\omega)=J(\omega\mid\omega+d)$. The correction equals $1$ and the acceptance ratio reduces to the ratio of target densities.

title: Survival from the hazard
body: Why is the integration constant zero in $\log S(t)=-H(t)$?
answer: An absolutely continuous nonnegative lifetime has $P(T=0)=0$, so $S(0)=1$ and $\log S(0)=0$. An atom at zero would require its own initial survival factor.

title: Five years of a component
body: Find survival through five years for the constant hazard $0.1$ per year.

title: How many distinct heights?
body: For four clinics and three merges, what is the largest number of distinct cophenetic values the dendrogram can contain, and how many pairs are there?
answer: There are $6$ pairs and at most $3$ distinct cophenetic values, one per merge. In the average-linkage tree the distinct values are $1$, $2$, and $10.5$.

title: Complete-linkage average
body: The six cophenetic values under complete linkage are $1$, $2$, and four copies of $12$. What is their average?

title: A cut
body: Under average linkage, does a cut at height $6$ return two clusters or one?
answer: Height $6$ lies between $2$ and $10.5$, so the two pairs have been formed and have not yet been joined. The cut returns two clusters.

title: What is the hinge at margin $0.2$, and what is the slope of the hinge, as a function of the margin, just to the left of $1$?
body: What is the hinge at margin $0.2$, and what is the slope of the hinge, as a function of the margin, just to the left of $1$?
answer: The hinge is $1-0.2=0.8$. Just to the left of $1$ the slope in the margin is $-1$.

title: In the criterion above, take $\lambda=2$ and $\lVert\beta\rVert=1$, and add the penalty to the worked total hinge of $2.25$.
body: In the criterion above, take $\lambda=2$ and $\lVert\beta\rVert=1$, and add the penalty to the worked total hinge of $2.25$. What is the criterion value?
answer: The penalty is $(2/2)(1)=1$. The criterion value is $2.25+1=3.25$. A larger $\lambda$ charges the same weight more heavily and tolerates more hinge.

title: A longer fair interval
body:
Write the boundary values before solving the recurrence.

A fair walk between 0 and 8: calculate success probability and expected duration from five.
answer: The fair-walk solutions are $h_i=i/8$ and $e_i=i(8-i)$. At five they give success probability $5/8$ and mean duration $5\cdot3=15$ steps. Substitution into the first-step equations verifies both expressions.

title: An upward bias
body: A biased walk on four steps: use $p=2/3$ and start from one.
answer: Here $q/p=1/2$. The probability is $(1-1/2)/(1-1/16)=8/15$, compared with $1/4$ for the fair walk. The favourable upward transitions increase the chance of reaching four first.

title: An exit rate of $2$ per hour has already lasted $1$ hour.
body: An exit rate of $2$ per hour has already lasted $1$ hour. What is the probability that it lasts at least one further hour?
answer: Memorylessness makes the remaining wait a fresh exponential of rate $2$, so the probability is $e^{-2}\approx 0.1353$. The hour already spent does not appear in the answer.

title: Exit rates $3$ and $1$ leave a state.
body: Exit rates $3$ and $1$ leave a state. What is the probability that the rate-$3$ clock rings first, and what is the mean hold?
answer: The total rate is $4$, so the rate-$3$ clock wins with probability $3/4=0.75$. The mean hold is $1/4=0.25$ time unit.

title: For $n=6$, $p=2$, mean $(1,1)$ and $S=2I_2$, what is the transformed statistic?
body: For $n=6$, $p=2$, mean $(1,1)$ and $S=2I_2$, what is the transformed statistic?
answer: $2.4$. Here $T^2=6$ and the factor is $4/10=0.4$.

title: A statistic against an F quantile
body: Does $2.4$ exceed the $0.95$ quantile of $F_{2,4}$?
answer: No. That quantile is $6.944$. The upper tail probability of $2.4$ is $0.2066$.

title: When $p=1$, $n=5$, $\bar x=2$ and $s=1$, what is $T^2$?
body: When $p=1$, $n=5$, $\bar x=2$ and $s=1$, what is $T^2$?
answer: $20$, which equals $t^2$. The $F$ factor is $1$ in this one-dimensional case, so the transformed statistic is also $20$.

title: The three GLM components
body: Name the three components of a generalised linear model, and state the usual conditional-independence assumption.
answer: The components are an exponential-family distribution for the response, a linear predictor $\eta_i=x_i^{\mathsf T}\beta$, and a link $g(\mu_i)=\eta_i$. Responses are independent conditional on the covariates. For a normal response the usual link is the identity, so $\mu_i=\eta_i$.

title: Link, inverse link, and canonical link
body: What are a link function, an inverse link, and a canonical link?
answer: The link $g$ maps the conditional mean to the linear predictor, $g(\mu_i)=\eta_i$. The inverse link recovers the mean, $\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i)$. A canonical link equates $\eta_i$ with the natural parameter of the exponential family. For a normal mean that canonical link is the identity.

title: A zero in the table
body: $\Pr(X=1)=1/2$, $\Pr(Y=1)=1/3$ and $\Pr(X=1,Y=1)=0$. Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?
answer: No. The product of the marginals is $1/6$, and the joint probability is $0$. One cell where the product formula fails is enough.

title: A fair pair of coins
body: Two independent fair coins. Find $\Pr(\text{both heads})$ and $\E[XY]$ if a head is coded $1$ and a tail $0$.
answer: Each head has probability $1/2$, so both heads have probability $1/4$. That event is $\{XY=1\}$, and $XY$ is $0$ otherwise, so $\E[XY]=1/4$. This equals $\E[X]\E[Y]=(1/2)\times(1/2)$.

title: Counts under a constant rate
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Counts under a constant rate. Compute the count and first-wait probabilities.
answer: With rate three per hour, a half-hour count has mean $1.5$, so the probability of two is $e^{-1.5}1.5^2/2$. A first wait above one third of an hour has probability $e^{-1}$.

title: Stationary increments and changing levels
body: Stationary increments and changing levels. Distinguish the two distributions.
answer: A constant-rate process has $N(t+h)-N(t)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda h)$ for every start time. Its level $N(t)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda t)$ still depends on $t$.

title: A first wait and a window count
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

A first wait and a window count. Work both requested probabilities.
answer: The half-hour count has mean $1.5$, giving probability $e^{-1.5}1.5^2/2$ for exactly two events. Twenty minutes is one third of an hour, so the first-wait survival is $e^{-1}$.

title: Conditioning changes the experiment
body: Conditioning changes the experiment. Explain why the given count matters.
answer: Given $N(2)=3$ in a homogeneous process, the unordered arrival locations are independent uniforms over two hours. All three fall in the first hour with probability $(1/2)^3=1/8$.

title: Quartiles of a sample
body: A sample has first quartile 51 and third quartile 70. What is the interquartile range, and what is the upper 1.5-fence?
answer: The interquartile range is $70-51=19$. The upper fence is $70+1.5\times19=70+28.5=98.5$. An age beyond 98.5 would be drawn past the whisker. The fence is a drawing rule, not a statement that such an age is impossible.

title: A spread beside a mean
body: Creatinine quartiles are 0.9 and 1.4. Compute the interquartile range and the upper fence, and say why the mean can sit well above the median while this range stays small.
answer: The interquartile range is $1.4-0.9=0.5$. The upper fence is $1.4+1.5\times0.5=2.15$. A long right tail pulls the mean and the standard deviation and need not move $Q_1$ or $Q_3$ if the central order statistics stay put. That is the same mechanism as the value 100 leaving the interquartile range at 4.5.

title: Shared intercepts and slopes
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Shared intercepts and slopes. Explain where each random effect enters.
answer: A random intercept shifts a group’s baseline; a random slope changes its covariate effect. In a GLMM both enter the conditional linear predictor. Their covariance can make marginal dependence vary with the covariates.

title: A proposed negative correlation
body: A proposed negative correlation. Check the all-ones direction for four visits.
answer: The exchangeable matrix has all-ones eigenvalue $1+3\rho$. At $\rho=-0.5$ this is $-0.5$, so the matrix cannot be a correlation matrix. The lower permissible bound is $-1/3$.

title: A uniform interval
body:
Check the interval probabilities as well as the numerical transformation.

Draws from a uniform interval: transform $U$ into a uniform draw on $[10,15]$.
answer: Return $10+5U$. For $10\le x\le15$, its CDF is $\Pr\{U\le(x-10)/5\}=(x-10)/5$.

title: A cubic law
body: A cubic distribution function: for $F(x)=x^3$ on $[0,1]$, find the density, $\Pr(1/2<X<3/4)$ and the mean.
answer: The density is $3x^2$ on $(0,1)$. The interval probability is $27/64-1/8=19/64$, and integrating $x(3x^2)$ from zero to one gives mean $3/4$.

title: Why the normaliser cancels
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Why the normaliser cancels. Focus on the symmetric proposal and part (d).
answer: The forward and reverse proposal densities agree. The remaining target ratio divides two weights with the same normalising constant, so that constant cancels as well.

title: Successive states are related
body: Successive states are related. Compute the matrix-power entry.
answer: The two-step probability is $0.9(0.1)+0.1(0.6)=0.15$. A Markov chain can preserve a stationary law while successive states remain dependent.

title: Scoring as a weighted regression
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Scoring as a weighted regression. State the update and its representation.
answer: Fisher scoring uses $\beta_{new}=\beta+I(\beta)^{-1}S(\beta)$. In a GLM this is the solution of a weighted least-squares problem with the current working responses and weights.

title: Score covariance and curvature
body: Score covariance and curvature. Apply the Poisson log-link calculation requested there.
answer: The score is $X^\top(y-\mu)$, the Hessian is $-X^\top\operatorname{diag}(\mu)X$, and independent Poisson variances give that same matrix with positive sign as the score covariance.

title: The mean's standard error
body: Jackknife for a mean: derive the bias and standard error.
answer: $\widehat\theta_{(i)}=\bar x+(\bar x-x_i)/(n-1)$. Averaging makes the second term zero, so estimated bias is zero. The sum of squared deletion deviations is $s^2/(n-1)$; multiplying by $(n-1)/n$ and taking a square root gives $s/\sqrt n$.

title: Correcting a variance bias
body: The biased variance estimator: identify its leading bias term.
answer: The estimator is $(n-1)s^2/n$. Its expectation is $(1-1/n)\sigma^2$, so its bias is exactly $-\sigma^2/n$. For this statistic the delete-one bias correction recovers the unbiased sample variance, illustrating cancellation of a first-order term.

title: A larger joint table
body:
Sum actual nonzero cells before simplifying.

A joint table: calculate its margins and $E(X^2Y)$.
answer: The masses of $X=2,5,6$ are $0.2,0.2,0.6$. The masses of $Y=1,3,6,8$ are $0.2,0.3,0.2,0.3$. The zero mass at $(2,1)$ contradicts the product $0.2(0.2)$, so independence fails. Summing $x^2y$ times each cell gives $691/5=138.2$.

title: Combining elementary outcomes
body: Signs and their sum: which transformed pairs have positive mass?
answer: The pairs $(X,Y)=(1,2),(-1,0),(1,-2)$ have masses $1/16,6/16,9/16$. The middle cell combines two different sign outcomes. Hence $E(X)=1/4$, $E(Y)=-1$, and $E(XY)=-1$, giving covariance $-3/4$.

title: An absorbing state
body: All rates out of state $0$ are $0$. What is the jump chain's behaviour at $0$?
answer: $\nu_0=0$, so there is no next state. The holding time is infinite and the jump chain stays at $0$.

title: Two equal rates
body: $q_{12}=q_{13}=5$. Find the jump probabilities and the mean hold.
answer: $\nu_1=10$, so each destination has probability $5/10=1/2$. The mean holding time is $1/10$.

title: Separate a middle class from its tails
body:
Use the definitions and calculations above to work through these questions.

Separate a middle class from its tails. Use the square feature in the supplied map.
answer: The inner product expands to $(1+xx^{\prime})^2$. The middle class has square coordinate at most $0.81$ and the tails at least $2.25$, so the line at $1.5$ separates them in feature space.

title: A finite Gaussian Gram matrix
body: A finite Gaussian Gram matrix. Calculate its entries from pairwise distances.
answer: The matrix has diagonal one, adjacent entries $e^{-1/2}$ and corner entries $e^{-2}$. Its leading principal minors are positive, so it is positive definite for these three distinct inputs.

title: Margins and joints
body:
Practice question

Construct two pairs $(X,Y)$ with Bernoulli$(1/2)$ margins, one independent and one dependent. Compare $\mathrm{P}(X=Y)$.
answer: Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$. Then $\mathrm{P}(X=Y)=1/2$. The pair $(X,X)$ has the same margins, and $\mathrm{P}(X=X)=1$.

title: Which events distinguish two outcomes?
body:
Practice question

Let Ω={a,b,c,d} and F={∅,{a,b},{c,d},Ω}. Is X with values (2,2,3,3) measurable? Is Y with values (0,1,0,1) measurable? Exhibit a threshold event for each answer.
answer: X is measurable: for 2≤t<3, {X≤t}={a,b}, with ∅ below 2 and Ω at or above 3. All are in F. Y is not measurable: for 0≤t<1, {Y≤t}={a,c}, which is not in F. The same four numerical outcomes can support one measurement but not the other because F distinguishes only the two blocks.

title: Failure and repair
body:
Practice question

For the two-state chain with $\alpha=2$ and $\beta=3$, find the stationary distribution and $\mathbb{P}\bigl(X(t)=1\mid X(0)=0\bigr)$.
answer:
The stationary distribution on states $(0,1)$ is

$$
\pi=\Bigl(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta},\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\Bigr)=\Bigl(\frac{3}{5},\frac{2}{5}\Bigr).
$$

Starting from $0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}\bigl(X(t)=1\mid X(0)=0\bigr)=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\bigl(1-e^{-(\alpha+\beta)t}\bigr)=\frac{2}{5}\bigl(1-e^{-5t}\bigr).
$$

title: A generator row
body:
Practice question

Explain why the diagonal of a generator is non-positive and why each row sums to zero.
answer:
Off-diagonal rates $q_{ij}$ for $j
eq i$ are non-negative: they are rates of jumps. The diagonal entry is defined to be minus their sum, $q_{ii}=-
u_i\le 0$, which is the rate of leaving $i$. Each row then sums to $\sum_{j
eq i}q_{ij}+q_{ii}=0$. A row of probabilities would sum to $1$. A row of rates sums to $0$ because the outflow is recorded on the diagonal with a minus sign.

title: A zero that should be zero
body: Compute $D(p\,\Vert\,p)$ for $p=(0.8,0.2)$.
answer: Each ratio is $1$, and $\log 1=0$, so the divergence is $0$.

title: Which direction is larger?
answer: $D(q\,\Vert\,p)\approx 0.2231$ nats. The smaller number $0.1927$ is $D(p\,\Vert\,q)$, the penalty for using a fair coin when the truth is $p$.

title: Bits
body: The forward divergence is about $0.1927$ nats. Divide the unrounded value by $\log 2$ and round to four decimals. What is the result in bits?
answer: The unrounded divergence divided by $\log 2$ equals $0.2781$ bits.

title: Significance and adequacy
body:
Practice question

Does a significant predictor establish that a GLM fits adequately? Name one separate diagnostic check.
answer: **Definitions/notation.** A coefficient significance test addresses a specified null hypothesis about that coefficient within the assumed model; adequacy concerns whether the model describes the data sufficiently well. Significance does not establish adequacy: for example, inspect Pearson residuals $(y_i-\hat\mu_i)/\sqrt{\hat\phi V(\hat\mu_i)}$ against fitted values for unexplained patterns or changing spread.

title: A saturated comparison
body:
Practice question

What is a saturated model, and what does deviance compare? Distinguish deviance from scaled deviance.
answer: **Definitions/notation.** A saturated mean model fits each observed response exactly ($\tilde\mu_i=y_i$, possibly as a boundary limit); at common dispersion $\phi$, the scaled deviance is $D/\phi=2\{\ell(\tilde\mu;y,\phi)-\ell(\hat\mu;y,\phi)\}$. Thus the unscaled deviance $D$ is $\phi$ times that log-likelihood-ratio discrepancy, and equals the scaled deviance when $\phi=1$.

title: Label switching
body: What must be exchanged along with the component means?
answer: Exchange the weights, variances, and every other component-specific parameter at the same time. The sums defining the mixture density then contain exactly the same terms.

title: Mean and variance of a mixture
body: For weights $(0.3,0.7)$, means $(0,4)$ and variances $(1,4)$, compute the mixture mean and variance.
answer: The mean is $2.8$. The within-component variance is $3.1$ and the between-component variance is $3.36$, giving total variance $6.46$. Permuting complete components leaves all three quantities unchanged.

title: The scalar Gaussian factor
body: The Laplace integral: evaluate it and identify its sample-size factor.
answer: Set $z=\sqrt h(\theta-\widetilde\theta)$. The integral becomes $h^{-1/2}\sqrt{2\pi}$. If $h=nI_1$, its logarithm is $-\tfrac12\log n+\tfrac12\log(2\pi/I_1)$, displaying the one-parameter contribution to the log marginal likelihood penalty.

title: Updating model odds
body: Bayes factor and posterior probability: convert the supplied Bayes factor to posterior odds.
answer: Prior odds are $0.25/0.75=1/3$. Multiplication by the Bayes factor $6$ gives posterior odds $2$, hence posterior probability $2/(1+2)=2/3$. A marginal likelihood ratio changes prior model odds; it is not itself a posterior probability.

title: The multiplier
body: For $E(w)=(w-3)^2$, which constant learning rates make the error shrink at every step?
answer: Those with $0<\varepsilon<1$. The absolute value of $1-2\varepsilon$ is then below $1$. At $\varepsilon=1$ the error keeps its size and changes sign.

title: Two steps from 5
body: From $w=5$ with $\varepsilon=0.4$, what are the next two weights?
answer: The multiplier is $0.2$. The error $2$ becomes $0.4$, so the first weight is $3.4$. The error $0.4$ becomes $0.08$, so the second weight is $3.08$.

title: A finite sum of steps
body: Why can $\gamma_r=1/r^2$ fail a descent that $\gamma_r=1/r$ is built to finish?
answer: The sum $\sum 1/r^2$ converges, so the total distance the updates are allowed to travel is finite. The schedule can stop short of the minimiser. The harmonic schedule $\sum 1/r$ diverges, so the total step length is unlimited, while $\sum 1/r^2$ still converges.

title: For $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$, $(2,4)$, what is the fitted height at $x=1$?
body: For $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$, $(2,4)$, what is the fitted height at $x=1$?
answer: $2$, the mean of $y$. The arithmetic is $0.5+1.5\cdot 1=2$.

title: What is the origin-constrained slope for these three points?
body: What is the origin-constrained slope for these three points?
answer: $9/5=1.8$. The products $x_i y_i$ sum to $9$ and the squares $x_i^2$ sum to $5$.

title: Why is the origin line's residual sum of squares $1.8$ rather than $1.5$?
body: Why is the origin line's residual sum of squares $1.8$ rather than $1.5$?
answer: The origin line is not allowed an intercept. The free line reaches $1.5$ by using intercept $0.5$. Inside the origin-only family, $1.8$ is the minimum.

title: One leverage
body: A least-squares fit has ordinary residual $-0.3$ and leverage $1/4$ at a case. Find the leave-one-out residual.
answer: Divide by $1-1/4=3/4$. The leave-one-out residual is $-0.3/(3/4)=-0.4$.

title: Training residual against leave-one-out
body: In the three-point line, the mean squared ordinary residual is $0.5$ and the mean squared leave-one-out error is $6.75$. Why is the second number the one that estimates prediction error?
answer: Each ordinary residual scores a point on a line that used that point. Each leave-one-out residual scores the point on the line fitted to the other two. The average of those three squared residuals estimates the expected squared error of the fitting rule on a new case. The ordinary residual average estimates how well the line interpolates its own sample.

title: A shared training set
body: Two leave-one-out training sets from a sample of size $20$ each omit a different row. How many training rows do they share, and why does that block a binomial standard error for the average of the $20$ errors?
answer: They share $18$ rows. The $20$ held-out errors are functions of heavily overlapping fits, so they are dependent. A binomial variance $p(1-p)/20$ would treat them as independent indicators and would overstate the precision of the average.

title: A probability of two successes
body:
Practice question

In three independent Bernoulli trials let T be the success count. Show that h(T)=T(T-1)/6 is unbiased for p², and evaluate it at T=2. Why is this function unique among unbiased functions of T when p ranges over (0,1)?
answer: There are six ordered pairs of distinct trials. Each pair succeeds with probability p², so E[T(T-1)/6]=p². At T=2 the estimate is 2/6=1/3. If another function of T were unbiased for p², its difference from h would have expectation zero for every p. The binomial count is complete on (0,1), so the difference is zero almost surely.

title: Conditioning an estimator
body:
Practice question

Let $U$ be unbiased for $\theta$ and let $T$ be sufficient. In one sentence each, say why $W(T)=\mathbb{E}(U\mid T)$ is a statistic, why it is unbiased, and why $\operatorname{Var} W\le\operatorname{Var} U$.
answer: $W(T)$ is a statistic because sufficiency makes the conditional distribution of the sample given $T$ free of $\theta$, so the conditional expectation does not depend on $\theta$. It is unbiased because $\mathbb{E}\{W(T)\}=\mathbb{E}(U)=\theta$ by the tower property. Its variance is smaller because $\operatorname{Var}(U)=\operatorname{Var}\{W(T)\}+\mathbb{E}\{\operatorname{Var}(U\mid T)\}$ and the second term is nonnegative.

title: The hundred tosses
body: For $100$ fair tosses, what are the exact probability $\mathrm{P}(S\ge 60)$, the plain normal approximation, and the continuity-corrected approximation, to four decimals?
answer: The exact value is $0.0284$. The plain approximation is $0.0228$. The continuity correction is $0.0287$.

title: Chebyshev against the normal tail
body: The Chebyshev bound on $\mathrm{P}(|S/100-1/2|\ge 0.1)$ is $0.25$. Why is that not a contradiction of the normal tail near $0.023$?
answer: Chebyshev's inequality is an upper bound that uses only the variance. The normal approximation estimates the probability. An upper bound of $0.25$ is compatible with a probability near $0.046$ for the two tails.

title: Twenty tosses
body: For $S\sim\mathrm{Bin}(20,1/2)$, the exact $\mathrm{P}(S\le 8)$ is $0.2517$ and the plain normal value is $0.186$. What does the continuity correction do?
answer: It reads the normal distribution at $8.5$ rather than at $8$, and the value is about $0.251$, close to $0.2517$. The plain reading at $8$ is the one that sits low.

title: Transforming a uniform input
body:
Practice question

Explain how to generate a draw from the uniform distribution on $[10,15]$, starting from a uniform draw on $[0,1]$.
answer: Draw $U\sim\operatorname{U}[0,1]$ and return $X=10+5U$.

title: Transforming to a waiting time
body:
Practice question

Explain how to generate a draw from the exponential distribution with rate $10$, starting from a uniform draw on $[0,1]$.
answer: Draw $U\sim\operatorname{U}[0,1]$ and return $X=-\log(U)/10$. This is the inverse-transform method: the distribution function $1-e^{-10x}$ inverts to $-\log(1-u)/10$, and $1-U$ has the same distribution as $U$.

title: A zero predictor
body: Give the identity, log and logit means at $\eta=0$.
answer: The identity mean is $0$. The log-link mean is $e^{0}=1$. The logit mean is $1/2$. Zero is a legal log mean only in the limit $\eta\to-\infty$; at $\eta=0$ the log mean is $1$.

title: A coefficient on the log scale
body: Under a log link, $\eta=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$ and $\beta_1=0.2$. By what factor does the mean change when $x$ increases by $1$?
answer: The mean is multiplied by $e^{0.2}=1.2214$ to four decimals. The identity link would have added $0.2$ instead of multiplying.

title: A server completes $12$ jobs an hour, and the mean number of jobs in the system is $3$.
body: A server completes $12$ jobs an hour, and the mean number of jobs in the system is $3$. What is the mean sojourn, in minutes?
answer: $W=3/12=1/4$ hour, which is $15$ minutes. The completion rate in a stable system is the accepted arrival rate.

title: The mean wait in the queue is $10$ minutes and the mean service is $5$ minutes, with $12$ jobs an hour accepted.
body: The mean wait in the queue is $10$ minutes and the mean service is $5$ minutes, with $12$ jobs an hour accepted. What are $L_q$ and $L$?
answer: Ten minutes is $1/6$ hour and five minutes is $1/12$ hour, so $W=1/6+1/12=1/4$ hour. Then $L_q=12\times 1/6=2$ and $L=12\times 1/4=3$.

title: Pairs and means
body: For a set of $N$ points with mean $\bar x$, why is $\sum_i\sum_l\|x_i-x_l\|^2=2N\sum_i\|x_i-\bar x\|^2$?
answer: Expand $\|x_i-x_l\|^2=\|x_i-\bar x\|^2+\|x_l-\bar x\|^2-2(x_i-\bar x)^{\mathsf T}(x_l-\bar x)$. The cross term sums to zero because the deviations from the mean sum to zero. Each squared deviation is then counted $2N$ times.

title: Counting partitions
body: How many ways are there to split $\{1,2,3,4\}$ into two nonempty unlabelled clusters, and what is $S(10,3)$?
answer: There are seven splits: four of type $1\mid 3$ and three of type $2\mid 2$. The Stirling number $S(10,3)$ equals $9330$.

title: In the worked correlation matrix, what fraction of the standardised variance is left for the second component?
body: In the worked correlation matrix, what fraction of the standardised variance is left for the second component?
answer: The eigenvalues sum to the trace $2$, so the second component accounts for $0.2/2=0.1$.

title: A unit loading of $0.6$ belongs to a component of variance $0.25$.
body: A unit loading of $0.6$ belongs to a component of variance $0.25$. What is the correlation between that variable and the score?
answer: The correlation is $0.6\sqrt{0.25}=0.6\times 0.5=0.3$.

title: For the distribution $(4/7,2/7,1/7)$ above, what is $\pi_2/\pi_1$, and which rate ratio must it equal?
body: For the distribution $(4/7,2/7,1/7)$ above, what is $\pi_2/\pi_1$, and which rate ratio must it equal?
answer: $\pi_2/\pi_1=(1/7)/(2/7)=1/2$, and the cut says this equals $\lambda_1/\mu_2=1/2$.

title: If $\lambda_n=1$ and $\mu_n=1$ for every $n\ge 1$, can the product weights be scaled to a probability on $\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$?
body: If $\lambda_n=1$ and $\mu_n=1$ for every $n\ge 1$, can the product weights be scaled to a probability on $\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$?
answer: No. Every weight equals $\pi_0$, and $\sum_n 1$ diverges. The equations still define an invariant measure.

title: A zero predictor
body: Give the logit and probit probabilities at $\eta=0$, and the complementary log-log probability to four decimals.
answer: The logit and the probit both equal $1/2$. Complementary log-log equals $1-\exp(-1)=0.6321$ to four decimals. Symmetry about $1/2$ fails at the origin for that link.

title: A large positive predictor
body: As $\eta\to\infty$, what happens to each of the three probabilities?
answer: Each tends to $1$. The logit ratio $e^{\eta}/(1+e^{\eta})$ does, $\Phi(\eta)$ does, and $\exp(-e^{\eta})$ tends to $0$, so complementary log-log tends to $1$. The limits agree; the speed at a finite $\eta$ does not.

title: An M/M/1 queue
body: Arrivals are $2$ per hour and service is $3$ per hour. Find $\pi_0$, $\Pr(N\ge 3)$, $L$, and $W$.

title: An M/M/∞ system
body: Arrivals are $6$ per hour and each service rate is $2$ per hour, with infinitely many servers. Find the stationary mean and the probability that the system is empty.
answer: The mean is $\lambda/\mu=3$. The empty-system probability is the Poisson probability $e^{-3}$. There is no requirement that $\lambda<\mu$.

title: Infinite servers
body: An M/M/∞ system: calculate its occupancy and sojourn measures.
answer: With $\lambda=6$ and $\mu=2$, $N$ is Poisson with mean $3$. Thus $P(N=0)=e^{-3}\approx0.049787$, $P(N\ge4)=1-e^{-3}(1+3+9/2+27/6)\approx0.352768$, and $W=1/2$ hour. There is no waiting before service.

title: Balancing neighbouring states
body: Birth–death balance on three states: normalise the local-balance weights.
answer: The equations are $\pi_0=\pi_1/3$ and $(2/3)\pi_1=\pi_2$. Weights $(1,3,2)$ solve them and sum to six, giving $(1/6,1/2,1/3)$. The same flow idea yields factorial weights in the infinite-server process, where the downward rate changes with state.

title: Pilot weights
body:
Keep the full width, half-width, and assumed critical value distinct.

Narrowing a pilot interval: use the pilot half-width to plan the new size.
answer: The half-width is $(82.5-59.3)/2=11.6$ at size $100$. Holding the variance estimate and critical value fixed gives $n\geq100(11.6/1)^2=13456$.

title: Weekend sleep
body: Hours of sleep: use the question's fixed normal approximation.
answer: The target size is at least $4(7.39/2)^2=54.6121$. Rounding upward gives $55$. The calculation uses the fixed estimated standard deviation and critical value specified in the question.

title: Conditional versus marginal effects
body: In one sentence each, say what a logistic random-intercept coefficient and a population-average coefficient describe, and why they need not match.
answer: The logistic random-intercept coefficient is a log-odds change at a fixed random intercept. The population-average coefficient describes the marginal mean after the random intercept has been averaged out. Because the inverse logit is nonlinear, the average of the conditional probabilities is not the conditional probability at the average intercept, so the two coefficients describe different contrasts. In the two-point example those contrasts are a log-odds change of 1 and a probability change of 0.1904.

title: Generalised estimating equations
body: What does a generalised estimating equation estimate, and what does it not require?
answer: It estimates the coefficients of a marginal mean for correlated responses, using the derivative of that mean and a working within-cluster covariance. It does not require a full joint distribution of the responses inside a cluster. Consistency of the coefficient, under the usual regularity conditions, needs a correct marginal mean and independent clusters. It does not need the working covariance to be the true one. A sandwich variance is the corresponding uncertainty statement.

title: Precision to graph
body: For the precision matrix above, what is $\Sigma=K^{-1}$, and what are the partial correlations?
answer:
$\det K=8$ and
$$
\Sigma=\frac18\begin{pmatrix}5&2&1\\2&4&2\\1&2&5\end{pmatrix}.
$$
The partial correlations are $1/\sqrt{6}\approx 0.408$ for the two edges and $0$ for the missing edge. The marginal correlation of $X_1$ and $X_3$ is $0.2$.

title: Cliques and separators
body: On the graph with edges $12,13,23,24,34,45,46,56$, what is the boundary of $\{1,2\}$, and is $\{2\}$ a separator of $1$ and $4$?
answer: The boundary of $\{1,2\}$ is $\{3,4\}$. The set $\{2\}$ does not separate $1$ from $4$, because the path $1-3-4$ avoids $2$. One global statement is $X_{\{1,2,3\}}\perp X_{\{5,6\}}\mid X_4$.

title: Reading the graph
body: On the path $X-Y-Z$, which pair is conditionally independent given the third variable, and which pairs are neighbours?
answer: $X$ and $Z$ are the non-adjacent pair, so the pairwise property says $X\perp Z\mid Y$. The edges are $X-Y$ and $Y-Z$. The pairwise property does not say that an adjacent pair is conditionally independent given the remaining variable.

title: A numerical check of the margin
body: Using the worked example, compute $\Pr(X=1,Z=0)$.
answer: Given $Y=1$ the probability is $0.8\times 0.2=0.16$. Given $Y=0$ it is $0.2\times 0.8=0.16$. The marginal is $\tfrac12(0.16)+\tfrac12(0.16)=0.16$.

title: The hour-long job
body: A nonnegative duration has mean $10$ minutes. What does Markov's inequality say about a duration of at least $60$ minutes?
answer: The probability is at most $10/60=1/6$. If the variance is $25$, Chebyshev's inequality further bounds the same event by $25/50^2=0.01$.

title: Equality
body: Construct a nonnegative law with mean $4$ for which $\mathrm{P}(X\ge 20)=0.2$.
answer: Put probability $0.2$ on $20$ and probability $0.8$ on $0$. The mean is $4$ and the tail probability equals $0.2$, so Markov's bound is attained.

title: An exponential tail
body: For an exponential law with mean $10$, compute $e^{-6}$ to six decimals and compare it with $1/6$.
answer: $e^{-6}\approx 0.002479$, while $1/6\approx 0.1667$. Markov's bound is valid and about $67$ times the exponential probability. The exponential number uses the survival formula. The Markov number uses only the mean.

title: The three GLM components
body: Name the three components of a generalised linear model and the usual conditional-independence assumption.
answer: An exponential-family response distribution, a linear predictor, and a link from the mean to that predictor. Responses are independent given the covariates. The likelihood fit estimates the coefficients in the linear predictor.

title: Link and canonical link
body: What is a link, and what is a canonical link?
answer: A link $g$ satisfies $g(\mu_i)=\eta_i$. A canonical link matches $\eta_i$ to the natural parameter. The log link is canonical for the Poisson mean, which is why the score in the worked example is $y-\mu$.

title: An observed association
body:
Practice question

The sample correlation between $\log_{10}$ serum creatinine and serum sodium in a heart-failure cohort is $-0.26$, and the correlation between $\log_{10}$ serum creatinine and age is $0.23$.

(a) Which pair moves together, and which pair moves in opposite directions?

(b) Why is neither correlation, by itself, a reason to conclude that one variable causes the other?

(c) The moment skewness of serum creatinine is about $4.4$ on its untransformed scale and $1.6$ after taking logarithms. Does the reduction in skewness prove that the transformed measurements are normally distributed?
answer:
(a) Serum creatinine and age move together: the correlation $0.23$ is positive, so older patients tend to have somewhat higher creatinine. Creatinine and sodium move in opposite directions: the correlation $-0.26$ is negative. Both are weak; a correlation of about $\pm0.25$ means a straight line accounts for only about 6% of the variance of either variable.

(b) A correlation measures linear association in this sample only. It can arise because a third variable drives both, here perhaps overall illness or kidney function, because the causal arrow points the other way, or by chance. These are observational data, so nothing was assigned and no causal reading follows from the correlation alone.

(c) No. A reduction from $4.4$ to $1.6$ still leaves positive moment skewness, and even zero skewness alone would not imply normality. A histogram or quantile plot is needed to examine shape more fully.

title: Estimating measurement variance
body:
Practice question

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be a random sample with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Show that $\sum_i (X_i-\overline X)^2=\sum_i (X_i-\mu)^2-n(\overline X-\mu)^2$, and deduce that $\mathbb{E} s^2=\sigma^2$.
answer:
Write $X_i-\overline X=(X_i-\mu)-(\overline X-\mu)$ and expand:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2-2(\overline X-\mu)\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)+n(\overline X-\mu)^2.
$$

Since $\sum(X_i-\mu)=n(\overline X-\mu)$, the middle term is $-2n(\overline X-\mu)^2$, which leaves $\sum(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\overline X-\mu)^2$.

Now $\mathbb{E}(X_i-\mu)^2=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb{E}(\overline X-\mu)^2=\operatorname{Var}\overline X=\sigma^2/n$. Hence

$$
\mathbb{E}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2=n\sigma^2-n\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=(n-1)\sigma^2,
$$

and $\mathbb{E} s^2=\sigma^2$.

title: A proposal cancellation
body:
Practice question

Why can Metropolis--Hastings use an unnormalised target? When do its proposal-density terms cancel?
answer: **Definitions/notation.** Let $\pi(z)=k(z)/Z$ be the target and $q(y\mid x)$ the proposal density from current state $x$ to candidate $y$. The acceptance probability is $\min\{1,k(y)q(x\mid y)/[k(x)q(y\mid x)]\}$ because $Z$ cancels; the proposal terms cancel only when $q(y\mid x)=q(x\mid y)$, as for a fixed-scale symmetric random walk.

title: Markov transitions and invariance
body:
Practice question

What is the Markov property? What does it mean for a distribution to be invariant for a chain?
answer: **Definitions/notation.** The Markov property says that the conditional distribution of the next state, given the whole past, depends only on the current state. A distribution $\pi$ is invariant if one transition preserves it: $X^{(t)}\sim\pi$ implies $X^{(t+1)}\sim\pi$; this alone does not establish convergence from every initial state.

title: One case
body: For the responses $1,3,5,7$ at $w=0$, what is the online gradient on the case $y=7$?
answer: The gradient is $0-7=-7$. It is an unbiased draw from the four case gradients $-1,-3,-5,-7$, whose mean is $-4$, but this particular draw is far from $-4$.

title: A deterministic partition
body: Why is the average of the gradients on $\{1,5\}$ and $\{3,7\}$ exactly $-4$, even though neither batch was drawn at random?
answer: The two batches partition the sample, so the average of their means is the mean of all four responses. Random sampling is not required for that identity. Unbiasedness of one batch requires the random draw.

title: A constant ratio
body: For the Poisson samples $(2,0,5)$ and $(1,3,3)$, what is the likelihood ratio, and does it depend on $\lambda$?
answer: The ratio is $36/240=0.15$ for every $\lambda>0$. The sums both equal $7$, so the powers of $\lambda$ cancel.

title: A ratio that moves
body: Evaluate $0.1\lambda^3$ at $\lambda=1$ and at $\lambda=2$.
answer: The values are $0.1$ and $0.8$. The ratio of $(2,0,5)$ against $(4,0,0)$ depends on $\lambda$, and the sums $7$ and $4$ differ.

title: A uniform window
body: Observations $0.2$, $0.9$, $1.1$ come from $\mathrm{Uniform}(\theta,\theta+1)$. For which $\theta$ is the likelihood positive?
answer: The parameter must satisfy $\theta\le 0.2$ and $\theta\ge 0.1$, so $\theta$ lies in $[0.1,0.2]$. The range $0.9$ does not determine this interval.

title: Three observed responses are $4$, $4$ and $10$, and one planned response is missing.
body: Three observed responses are $4$, $4$ and $10$, and one planned response is missing. What is the observed mean?
answer: The observed mean is $(4+4+10)/3=6$.

title: Why is inventing a mixture component label a different problem from estimating that missing response?
body: Why is inventing a mixture component label a different problem from estimating that missing response?
answer: The component label was never one of the intended measurements; it is part of a complete-data story. The missing response was a measurement the design meant to record. The two holes are filled by different models.
